The thickness of the compressor wall is a figure that has been the subject of considerable calculation, and once the corrosion allowance has been added to the thickness required by pressure considerations alone, the resulting wall thickness is 70 mm. It should be noted that the allowance represents a substantial part of this total, reflecting the corrosion behaviour that is expected on the gas side over the design life of the machine, and the figure as it stands is the one that will be passed to the fabricator for manufacture.

Attention is now turned to the question of the gaskets for the flanged joints, where a choice remains to be made between two candidate materials. It has been decided that the comparison between the two materials will be made on the basis of temperature limit only, and that other properties, including pressure rating, chemical resistance and cost, will be set aside for the purposes of this particular comparison. The reason for this approach is that the temperature limit is the property that actually constrains the design of the joint, since the flanges in the vicinity of the discharge experience the highest temperatures that occur anywhere in the machine.

When the two materials are compared on this basis, it is the material with the higher temperature rating that emerges as the preferred option. The material with the lower rating performs adequately under normal operating conditions, but difficulties arise in the excursion case, in which the discharge temperature rises for a period before the protective systems have had time to respond fully. A similar philosophy has in fact been adopted elsewhere in the design: the allowance that has been made for $\Delta P$ in the absorber circuit, and the margin that has been provided for NPSH at the lean solvent pump, have both been set by reference to the excursion case rather than the normal operating point, and the treatment of the gasket is consistent with the approach that has been taken in those areas, although the question of whether the seating requirements of the preferred material can be satisfied with the flange facing in its current form remains open and will need to be resolved before the preference can be regarded as

The compressor wall thickness is 70 mm once the corrosion allowance is added to the pressure-retaining thickness. The allowance is the larger part of the total: the pressure term alone leaves a wall thinner than the service allows, and the addition is set by the corrosion basis for the gas side. That basis is not reopened here. It was fixed with the materials selection for the absorber circuit, and the wall figure stands on it.

The gasket selection for the flanged joints remains open. Two materials are candidates, and the comparison is made on temperature limit only. Pressure rating, chemical resistance and cost stand outside the comparison, not because they are settled, but because temperature limit is the property on which the two materials differ in a way that binds the joint: the discharge flange sees the highest metal temperature in the machine, and the gasket at that flange must hold its seal at that temperature through each excursion.

On temperature limit the higher-rated material is preferred. The lower-rated material stays within its limit at the normal discharge temperature, and its weakness is the excursion, where the discharge temperature climbs while the protective response is still developing. A joint whose seal depends on the speed of that response has taken the gasket limit as an operating limit. The section has not accepted that dependence elsewhere: the $\Delta P$ allowance across the absorber and the NPSH margin at the lean solvent pump were both fixed against the excursion case rather than the normal point, and the gasket choice follows the same treatment.
